global.practical_note: Order-of-magnitude range reported across the literature spans ~10^5 to ~10^8 Gt CO2 (Kelemen et al. 2011, 2019) depending on whether the full peridotite/basalt rock volume within a few km of the surface is assumed reactive. NAS (2019) and Snæbjörnsdóttir et al. (2020) treat ~10^6 Gt as an order-of-magnitude 'rock volume x stoichiometry' theoretical ceiling — several orders of magnitude larger than any credible injectivity- or economics-limited practical capacity. No aggregated bottom-up global total (summing individually assessed formations) yet exists in the peer-reviewed literature; national/regional assessments (this file) cover only a small, non-representative fraction of global mafic/ultramafic rock volume.
sources: Snæbjörnsdóttir, S.Ó. et al. 2020. Carbon dioxide storage through mineral carbonation. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment 1, 90-102. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-019-0011-8

formations.name: Columbia River Basalt Group (Grande Ronde / Wallula)
formations.capacity_basis: Cao and colleagues (2024, PNNL) estimate 21-40 Gt CO2 for a 10,000 km2 study area in the Grande Ronde Basalt.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Stacked flood-basalt flows (Grande Ronde, Wanapum, Saddle Mountains) with porous, brecciated flow tops at 800-900+ m depth at Wallula. Dense flow interiors act as seals.
formations.suitability_notes: A well-characterized onshore basalt storage target, demonstrated at pilot scale.
formations.existing_activity: The Wallula pilot injected 977 t CO2 in 2013, and coring found up to 60% of it mineralized as ankerite within about 2 years; follow-on CarbonSAFE studies are ongoing.
formations.source: Cao, R. et al. 2024, Gigaton commercial-scale carbon storage and mineralization potential in stacked Columbia River basalt reservoirs, Int. J. Greenh. Gas Control 137, 104206, doi:10.1016/j.ijggc.2024.104206 (accepted manuscript https://www.osti.gov/pages/servlets/purl/2484726); McGrail, B.P. et al. 2006, Potential for carbon dioxide sequestration in flood basalts, J. Geophys. Res. 111, B12201, doi:10.1029/2005JB004169; McGrail et al. 2017 Environ. Sci. Technol. (Wallula results)
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Multiple stacked flood-basalt flows (Grande Ronde, Wanapum, Saddle Mountains) with permeable brecciated flow-top/interflow zones at 800-900+ m depth at Wallula; porosity concentrated in interflow rubble zones, dense flow interiors act as seals/reactive caprock.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Best-characterized onshore basalt storage target globally; demonstrated at pilot scale.
formations.existing_activity_research: Wallula Basalt Pilot (PNNL/Big Sky Carbon Sequestration Partnership): 977 t CO2 injected 2013; post-injection coring found up to 60% mineralized as ankerite within ~2 years. Follow-on 'Carbon TrapRock'/CarbonSAFE studies ongoing.
formations.capacity_basis_research: McGrail et al. 2006 conservative regional estimate 10-50 Gt CO2 (an earlier, less-cited McGrail 2006 figure of ~100 Gt also circulates). Later PNNL (2024, ScienceDirect 'Gigaton commercial-scale carbon storage...stacked Columbia River basalt reservoirs') estimates 36-148 Gt CO2 for the onshore Columbia River Basalt specifically (with much larger 500-2500 Gt offshore WA/BC and 1000-5500 Gt Caribbean flood-basalt figures reported in the same study as separate, more speculative provinces). High bound revised from 100 to 148 Gt to match the 2024 PNNL range; verified via web search July 2026. || 2026-10-15 verification: McGrail et al. 2006 (para 34): >100 Gt CO2 for whole CRBG (10 interflows x 10 m, 15% porosity, 100 atm). No 10-50 Gt figure exists in McGrail 2006; Matter & Kelemen 2009 attribute 36-148 Gt to McGrail 2006 but the paper does not contain it. Cao et al. 2024: accepted manuscript (OSTI 2484726) gives 21/35/40 Gt (DOE volumetric, At=10,000 km2); published abstract gives 181/304/351 Gt (P90/P50/P10) for the same study area; discrepancy unresolved (published full text not accessed). Verified 2026-10-15.

formations.name: Deccan Traps
formations.capacity_basis: Gorain and colleagues (2025) estimate 41-76 Gt CO2 for basalt deeper than 750 m in two sub-basins; Vishal and colleagues (2021) give up to 305 Gt for the whole province using a simpler pore-volume method.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Traps reach about 2 km thick in the Western Ghats, but porous flow tops are concentrated in the upper few hundred meters, often too shallow (under 800 m) for supercritical CO2. Dyke swarms compartmentalize flow.
formations.suitability_notes: A large theoretical resource, but a Princeton CMI (2022) synthesis found that "virtually none of it appears suitable for large-scale CO2 injection" because of shallow depth and dykes.
formations.existing_activity: Laboratory carbonation experiments on Deccan basalt cores (CSIR-NGRI, IIT Bombay); see also the IISER Bhopal/CSIR-NGRI research injection well.
formations.source: Gorain, S. et al. 2025, Assessment of carbon dioxide storage potential in Deccan basalts using geophysical methods, Discover Geoscience 3, 166, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44288-025-00259-7; Vishal, V. et al. 2021, A systematic capacity assessment and classification of geologic CO2 storage systems in India, Int. J. Greenh. Gas Control 111, 103458, doi:10.1016/j.ijggc.2021.103458; Princeton CMI 2022 'India's Deccan Traps Appear to Have Limited Capacity for Carbon Storage' https://cmi.princeton.edu/annual-meetings/annual-reports/year-2022-1/indias-deccan-traps-appear-to-have-limited-capacity-for-carbon-storage/
formations.capacity_basis_research: Vishal et al. (2021) estimate ~316 Gt CO2 combined Deccan Volcanic Province + Rajmahal Traps; subsequent reassessments (2022-2025, e.g. Princeton CMI summary, Discover Geoscience 2025) narrow practically accessible capacity to ~94-150 Gt given shallow depth and dense dyke networks that limit reservoir quality. A further probabilistic reassessment (2021-2025 systematic capacity assessment work incorporating porosity/net-to-gross/volumetric uncertainty) narrows this further to ~41-76 Gt CO2 (P10=43, P50=58, P90=74 Gt), suggesting the practical range may be lower than the 94-150 Gt figure retained here; flagged in verification_notes. || 2026-10-15 verification: Vishal et al. 2021 Table 6: DVP 94.00/243.50/304.88 Gt; Rajmahal 3.38/8.77/10.98 Gt; combined 97-316 Gt (abstract). Gorain et al. 2025: Monte Carlo 41-76 Gt (P10 43, P50 58, P90 74; their P10 = optimistic convention) for GRV 88,937 km3 below 750 m over 166,353 km2, NTG 19%, porosity 6-11%, 40.65 kg/m3 McGrail load. The previous '94-150 Gt practically accessible' figure had no traceable source and was removed. Note: Gorain section 5.9 text contains unfilled placeholders ('P10 = X Gt, P50 = Y Gt'); the abstract values are used. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Traps are up to ~2 km thick in the Western Ghats but reactive, porous flow-top zones are concentrated in the uppermost few hundred meters; many areas too shallow (<800 m) for supercritical CO2 injection; extensive vertical dyke swarms compartmentalize flow.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Large theoretical resource but 'virtually none of it appears suitable for large-scale CO2 injection' per Princeton CMI (2022) synthesis of Indian basalt studies, due to shallow depth/dyke compartmentalization; targeted formations (e.g. Eastern Deccan Volcanic Province, Killari-1 borehole area) show more promise.
formations.existing_activity_research: Laboratory carbonation experiments (CSIR-NGRI, IIT Bombay) on Deccan basalt cores; no field-scale pilot injection yet as of 2026.
formations.source_research: Vishal, V. et al. 2021 capacity assessment; Princeton CMI 2022 'India's Deccan Traps Appear to Have Limited Capacity for Carbon Storage' https://cmi.princeton.edu/annual-meetings/annual-reports/year-2022-1/indias-deccan-traps-appear-to-have-limited-capacity-for-carbon-storage/; Discover Geoscience 2025 https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44288-025-00259-7

formations.name: Rajmahal Traps
formations.capacity_basis: Vishal and colleagues (2021) estimate about 3-11 Gt CO2 for the Rajmahal Traps using a pore-volume method. A 450-600 m thick pile may lie largely above the depth needed for supercritical CO2, so this is an upper bound.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: An Early Cretaceous flood basalt pile about 450-600 m thick, with at least 28 lava flows of 20-70 m in its central part. It is much smaller and less studied than the Deccan.
formations.suitability_notes: A minor target relative to the Deccan, though regional mineral-trapping experiments sample nearby basalts.
formations.existing_activity: No known pilot.
formations.source: Vishal, V. et al. 2021, Int. J. Greenh. Gas Control 111, 103458, doi:10.1016/j.ijggc.2021.103458 (Table 6); McGrail, B.P. et al. 2006, J. Geophys. Res. 111, B12201, doi:10.1029/2005JB004169; ScienceDirect 2013 'CO2 Mineral Trapping: An Experimental Study on the Carbonation of Basalts from the Eastern Deccan Volcanic Province, India' https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1878522013001501
formations.capacity_basis_research: Included within combined ~316 Gt Vishal et al. 2021 Deccan+Rajmahal estimate; no disaggregated figure published. || 2026-10-15 verification: Vishal et al. 2021 Table 6: Rajmahal Traps (18,000 km2) 3.38/8.77/10.98 Gt; part of the combined 97-316 Gt basalt figure. Caveat: McGrail-type pore-volume load assumes ~1000 m depth; a 450-600 m exposed pile would not reach the ~750-800 m supercritical threshold unless buried (e.g., beneath Bengal Basin sediments).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Smaller, eastern Indian flood basalt province (~/100 m thick lava pile), Early Cretaceous age, less studied than Deccan. || 2026-10-15 verification: McGrail et al. 2006 para 36: Rajmahal trap 450-600 m thick basalt over ~18,000 km2; central part has at least 28 lava flows of 20-70 m (citing Klootwijk 1971). Replaces garbled '~/100 m'. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Minor target relative to Deccan; regional CO2 mineral trapping experiments (Eastern Deccan Volcanic Province studies) sample nearby basalts.
formations.source_research: Vishal, V. et al. 2021; ScienceDirect 2013 'CO2 Mineral Trapping: An Experimental Study on the Carbonation of Basalts from the Eastern Deccan Volcanic Province, India' https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1878522013001501

formations.name: Siberian Traps
formations.capacity_basis: No CO2 storage assessment exists, though an original extent of about 2-4 million km2 implies a very large theoretical resource.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: The lava pile is up to 3400 m thick in places (Tunguska Basin); permafrost and remoteness are major practical obstacles.
formations.suitability_notes: A very large continental flood basalt province, essentially unstudied for CO2 storage and far from industrial CO2 sources and infrastructure.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General LIP geology literature (Reichow et al. 2009 Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. on Siberian Traps volume/age)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated peer-reviewed CO2-storage capacity assessment identified; would be enormous given areal extent (largest continental flood basalt province on Earth, ~2-4 million km2 original extent) but is essentially unstudied for CCS/mineralization purposes.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Up to 3400 m thick lava pile in places (Tunguska Basin); permafrost terrain and remoteness are major practical obstacles.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Largest LIP globally by volume; a major data gap for the global inventory. No known industrial CO2 source co-location or infrastructure.
formations.source_research: General LIP geology literature (Reichow et al. 2009 Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. on Siberian Traps volume/age); no mineralization-specific capacity study found.

formations.name: Paraná-Etendeka Large Igneous Province
formations.capacity_basis: No basin-wide estimate is published; flow-through lab experiments (2024) reached about 75% carbonation within 72 hours, and subsurface mapping is laying the groundwork for capacity estimates.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: The Paraná portion covers about 1.2 million km2 with an average thickness of about 1.5 km (up to 2 km), and vesicular interflow zones provide reservoir-quality intervals. The African Etendeka portion is smaller and more eroded.
formations.suitability_notes: An emerging target close to Brazilian and Argentine industrial CO2 sources, with fast carbonation in lab experiments.
formations.existing_activity: No field pilot; subsurface geophysical and stratigraphic characterization was underway in 2024-2025.
formations.source: Rossetti, L. et al. 2025 Basin Research 'Subsurface Geology of the Paraná-Etendeka LIP' https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bre.70038; Scientific Reports 2024 'Unraveling the rapid CO2 mineralization experiment using the Paraná flood basalts' https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-58729-w
formations.capacity_basis_research: No basin-wide Gt figure yet published; Rossetti et al. 2025 (Basin Research) and 2024 EAGE paper provide subsurface geophysical characterization framing capacity work, and laboratory work (Scientific Reports 2024) shows ~75% carbonation efficiency (aragonite/dolomite/calcite) within 72 hours in flow-through experiments, supporting favorable reaction kinetics.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: South American (Paraná) portion ~1.2 x10^6 km2, ~1.5 km average thickness (up to 2 km), Early Cretaceous tholeiitic basalt; interflow/vesicular zones provide reservoir-quality intervals; African conjugate (Etendeka, Namibia/Angola) smaller, more eroded.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Emerging CCS target given proximity to Brazilian/Argentine industrial CO2 sources (steel, cement, refineries) and rapid experimental carbonation kinetics; subsurface stratigraphic mapping underway (2024-2025) as precursor to capacity estimates.
formations.existing_activity_research: No field pilot yet; active subsurface geophysical/stratigraphic characterization program (2024-2025).

formations.name: Karoo Large Igneous Province
formations.capacity_basis: No published estimate; the preserved Karoo basalt (Drakensberg Group) covers about 200,000 km2, far less than the province's original extent.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: The Early Jurassic lava pile is up to 1.4 km thick in the Lesotho highlands, with little subsurface characterization for CO2 storage.
formations.suitability_notes: Unstudied for CO2 storage in basalt, despite large coal-fired CO2 sources nearby in Mpumalanga.
formations.existing_activity: None known; South African CCS research has focused on sedimentary basins.
formations.source: General Karoo LIP volcanology literature (Duncan & Marsh 2006)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No published mineralization capacity estimate identified. Original Karoo/Ferrar LIP extent (with Antarctica) estimated at >3 x10^6 km2 but present-day exposed/preserved Karoo basalt (Drakensberg Group, Lesotho highlands) is much smaller (~200,000 km2).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Up to 1.4 km thick lava pile in Lesotho highlands (Drakensberg basalts), Early Jurassic age; limited subsurface reservoir characterization for CCS purposes.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Major data gap; South Africa has significant coal-fired CO2 point sources (Mpumalanga) that could pair with Karoo basalt/dolerite sills, but no dedicated CCS-in-basalt studies found.
formations.existing_activity_research: None known; South African CCS research (SACCCS) has focused primarily on sedimentary basins, not Karoo basalt mineralization.
formations.source_research: General Karoo LIP volcanology literature (Duncan & Marsh 2006); no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Ethiopian-Yemen Traps / Afar
formations.capacity_basis: No dedicated capacity study; the active Afar rift basalts are covered in the East African Rift, Ethiopia/Djibouti panel.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: An Oligocene (about 30 million years old) trap sequence up to 2 km thick in the northwest Ethiopian highlands, with highly fractured, shallower rift basalts near the Afar rift axis.
formations.suitability_notes: Large in extent but essentially unstudied for CO2 storage.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General geology (Hofmann et al. 1997 on Ethiopian flood basalt volcanism)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated capacity study found; Oligocene Ethiopian/Yemen flood basalts (~30 Ma) plus ongoing Afar rift volcanism give both LIP-scale flood basalt (flood_basalt) and active rift basalt (rift_volcanic) targets - see separate 'East African Rift - Ethiopia/Djibouti' entry for the rift-related component.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Up to 2 km thick trap sequence in NW Ethiopian highlands; highly fractured Afar rift basalts at shallower depth near the rift axis.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Large areal extent, essentially unstudied for CCS; overlaps with active East African Rift basalt category below.
formations.source_research: General geology (Hofmann et al. 1997 on Ethiopian flood basalt volcanism); no CO2 storage capacity study identified.

formations.name: North Atlantic Igneous Province (Faroe Islands / Vøring & Møre margins)
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity estimate has been published for these basalts. Reservoir studies are at an early research stage.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Onshore Faroe Islands basalt shows porosity of 0.5-36.2%, highest in brecciated flow-top crusts, with permeability up to about 10^-12 m2 (Rosenqvist and colleagues 2023). Buried equivalents on the Vøring and Møre margins are known from offshore drilling such as ODP hole 642E.
formations.suitability_notes: Studied by the University of Oslo's CO2Basalt project as a novel offshore reservoir that could pair with Norwegian CO2 hubs such as Northern Lights.
formations.existing_activity: Research-stage characterization only (CO2Basalt project, University of Oslo); no injection pilot.
formations.source: Rosenqvist, M.P. et al. 2023, Reservoir properties and reactivity of the Faroe Islands Basalt Group: Investigating the potential for CO2 storage in the North Atlantic Igneous Province, Int. J. Greenh. Gas Control, doi:10.1016/j.ijggc.2023.103838; UiO Njord CO2Basalt project https://www.mn.uio.no/njord/english/research/projects/co2-basalts/index.html
formations.capacity_basis_research: No basin-wide Gt figure yet published for the NAIP specifically; the broader claim that 'mid-ocean-ridge and oceanic basalt systems worldwide could store up to ~100,000 Gt CO2' (SINTEF/NORDICCS synthesis) is sometimes applied to NAIP margins by extension, but this is a global-ridge figure, not an NAIP-specific assessment.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Faroe Islands Basalt Group reservoir study (Rosenqvist et al. 2023) finds porosity 0.5-36.2% concentrated in brecciated/vesicular flow-top crusts (individual flows 0.6-18.5 m thick at the 642E borehole, Vøring Margin); permeability up to ~10^-12 m2 in least-altered crusts; more altered basalt is markedly less reactive/permeable.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Targeted by Norwegian (Njord/CO2Basalt project, University of Oslo) research as a novel offshore CCS reservoir type distinct from saline aquifers; would pair with North Sea/Norwegian CO2 capture hubs (Northern Lights etc.) if developed.
formations.existing_activity_research: Research-stage characterization only (CO2Basalt project, Njord Centre, Univ. of Oslo); no injection pilot.
formations.source_research: Rosenqvist, M.P. et al. 2023, 'Reservoir Properties and Reactivity of the Faroe Islands Basalt Group', Int. J. Greenhouse Gas Control, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1750583623000087; Njord CO2Basalt project https://www.mn.uio.no/njord/english/research/projects/co2-basalts/index.html; Geoforskning.no 'Can we store CO2 in Norway's offshore lava flows?'

formations.name: Emeishan Large Igneous Province
formations.depth_porosity_notes: A Permian flood basalt province in southwest China (Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou), up to 5 km thick in the inner zone and poorly characterized as a CO2 reservoir.
formations.suitability_notes: Unstudied for CO2 mineralization; Chinese storage research has concentrated on sedimentary basins such as the Ordos and Sichuan.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General LIP literature (Xu et al. 2004 on Emeishan volcanism)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 mineralization capacity study identified in literature searched.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Permian flood basalt province in SW China (Sichuan/Yunnan/Guizhou), up to 5 km thick in the inner zone; poorly characterized for CCS reservoir properties.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Data gap; China has strong CCS/CCUS policy interest but published work concentrates on sedimentary basin storage (Ordos, Sichuan Basin sandstones), not Emeishan basalt mineralization.
formations.source_research: General LIP literature (Xu et al. 2004 on Emeishan volcanism); no capacity study identified.

formations.name: Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) - Eastern North America / Morocco
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity estimate; the original province was vast, but the remaining basalts in the eastern US and Morocco are limited in extent and only hundreds of meters thick.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Eastern US basalts (Watchung, Palisades) are typically under 300 m thick and often near the surface, too shallow for supercritical CO2; Moroccan basalts are similarly thin.
formations.suitability_notes: Likely of limited practical relevance because the basalts are thin and shallow, despite proximity to dense US East Coast CO2 sources.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General CAMP literature (Marzoli et al. 1999 Science)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated capacity estimate identified; CAMP (Triassic-Jurassic, ~201 Ma) is one of the largest LIPs by original areal extent (>10^7 km2 including now-separated continents) but present-day exposed basalt (Newark, Hartford, Culpeper basin traps in eastern USA; Morocco's High Atlas basalts) is comparatively limited and thin (100s of m).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Eastern US CAMP basalts (e.g. Watchung/Palisades) are typically <300 m thick, often near-surface (unsuitable depth for supercritical CO2 without deeper equivalents); Moroccan CAMP basalts similarly thin.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Likely limited practical relevance vs. other LIPs due to thinness/shallow depth, but included for completeness given proximity to dense US East Coast CO2 sources.
formations.source_research: General CAMP literature (Marzoli et al. 1999 Science); no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Samail Ophiolite (Oman / UAE)
formations.capacity_basis: Kelemen and Matter (2008) estimate that fully carbonating the Samail peridotite would store about 30,000 Gt CO2; the wider literature range of 10,000-100,000 Gt depends on the assumed reactive fraction and depth.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Peridotite in this very large exposed ophiolite is at the surface and extends several km deep, including offshore beneath thin sediment. Natural carbonation forming travertine and carbonate veins shows the reactions are fast.
formations.suitability_notes: A major in-situ mineralization target, with enhanced carbonation proposed to reach over 1 Gt CO2 per year in Oman alone (Kelemen and Matter 2008).
formations.existing_activity: 44.01 is injecting CO2 into peridotite at pilot scale, and Oman Drilling Project boreholes are used for carbonation-rate studies.
formations.source: Kelemen, P.B. & Matter, J. 2008. PNAS 105(45):17295-300 https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0805794105; Kelemen et al. 2011 Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci.; Mervine et al. 2014 GCA (14C carbonation ages) https://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/sites/default/files/u988/2014%20Mervine%20et%20al%20GCA%2014C%20Oman%20carbonates.pdf; JPT/SPE 2023 coverage of 44.01
formations.capacity_basis_research: Kelemen & Matter 2008 PNAS: ~50x10^12 tonnes of peridotite in the Samail massif could mineralize ~30x10^12 t CO2 (30,000 Gt) if fully carbonated; wider literature range (Kelemen et al. 2011/2019 syntheses) of 10^4-10^5 Gt depending on assumed reactive fraction/depth cutoff.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: World's largest and best-exposed on-land ophiolite (obducted oceanic crust+mantle); peridotite (harzburgite/dunite) exposed at surface to several km depth; natural carbonation already forms travertine terraces and carbonate veins (14C ages ~26,000 yr average, up to Holocene) demonstrating rapid natural reaction kinetics; also present offshore beneath thin sediment cover in the Gulf of Oman.
formations.suitability_notes_research: The flagship global ISM target in the literature; natural CO2 uptake estimated to already consume >10,000-100,000 t CO2/yr passively, with in-situ enhanced carbonation (fracturing, heating, elevated pCO2) proposed to reach >1 Gt CO2/yr in Oman alone (Kelemen & Matter 2008).
formations.existing_activity_research: 44.01 (Omani startup, backed by Actis, XPRIZE Carbon Removal winner 2023) actively injecting CO2 into peridotite at pilot scale in the Fizh/Samail massif; academic Oman Drilling Project boreholes used for carbonation-rate studies.

formations.name: New Caledonia Peridotite Nappe
formations.capacity_basis: A very large peridotite body (about 150 by 40 km), but no capacity figure specific to New Caledonia is published.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Heavily serpentinized and weathered at the surface (a major nickel ore source), with active natural carbonation forming magnesite veins and offshore carbonate chimneys.
formations.suitability_notes: A strong natural analogue for in-situ carbonation, with an offshore extension beneath thin sediment that could ease injection siting.
formations.existing_activity: No CCS pilot; studied academically for natural carbonation.
formations.source: Kelemen, P.B. et al. Frontiers 2019 status/challenges review https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/climate/articles/10.3389/fclim.2019.00009/full; Quesnel, B. et al. 2013 'Syn-tectonic, meteoric water-derived carbonation of the New Caledonia Peridotite Nappe'
formations.capacity_basis_research: Kelemen et al. (Frontiers 2019 and related syntheses) note the New Caledonia massif (~150 x 40 km) is one of the world's largest peridotite bodies; converting all Mg cations to carbonate across combined large ophiolites (New Caledonia + PNG) discussed at the ~77,000 Gt (77x10^12 t) scale in aggregate, but no New-Caledonia-specific disaggregated number published.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Obducted oceanic mantle peridotite (harzburgite/dunite), extensively serpentinized and lateritized at surface (source of world-class Ni ore); documented active natural carbonation (magnesite veins, offshore alkaline carbonate-chimney spring) since the Oligocene.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Strong natural analogue for in-situ carbonation given documented active magnesite-forming systems; offshore extension beneath thin sediment noted by Kelemen et al. as advantageous for injection infrastructure siting.
formations.existing_activity_research: No CCS pilot; studied academically for natural carbonation processes (meteoric-water-driven listwanite/magnesite formation).

formations.name: Papua New Guinea Ophiolite Belt
formations.capacity_basis: A very large ophiolite (about 200 by 50 km, the Papuan Ultramafic Belt), with no published capacity figure.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Cretaceous oceanic crust and mantle thrust onto land, with peridotite extending offshore beneath thin sediment, similar to Oman and New Caledonia.
formations.suitability_notes: Geologically world-class but remote, with limited infrastructure and no CCS development.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: Kelemen, P.B. et al. Frontiers 2019 https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/climate/articles/10.3389/fclim.2019.00009/full
formations.capacity_basis_research: Cited by Kelemen et al. as one of the world's largest ophiolites (~200 x 50 km, Papuan Ultramafic Belt); no disaggregated Gt figure published separately from Oman/New Caledonia comparisons.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Papuan Ultramafic Belt - obducted Cretaceous oceanic crust/mantle sequence; peridotite present beneath thin sedimentary cover offshore, similar to Oman and New Caledonia.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Remote, limited infrastructure; flagged in the academic literature as geologically world-class but essentially undeveloped for CCS.

formations.name: Zambales Ophiolite (Philippines)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: An Eocene-Oligocene ophiolite on Luzon with partially serpentinized harzburgite and dunite and associated chromite deposits.
formations.suitability_notes: One of several Southeast Asian ophiolite belts that are geologically analogous to Oman but unstudied for CO2 storage.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Philippine ophiolite geology literature (Yumul et al. reviews)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated capacity study found.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Eocene-Oligocene ophiolite complex (Zambales Range, Luzon) with harzburgite, dunite, and associated chromite deposits; partially serpentinized.
formations.suitability_notes_research: One of several SE Asian ophiolite belts (with Palawan, Mindanao) that are geologically analogous to Oman but entirely unstudied for CO2 storage as of this compilation.
formations.source_research: General Philippine ophiolite geology literature (Yumul et al. reviews); no mineralization study identified.

formations.name: Troodos Ophiolite (Cyprus)
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity estimate; short lab tests found only 0.7% carbonation in unmilled samples, rising to 7.4% with milling, illustrating slow reaction rates.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: A classic, well-preserved Cretaceous ophiolite with extensive harzburgite and dunite; variable serpentinization controls reactivity.
formations.suitability_notes: Long studied as an ophiolite type locality, but no field-scale CO2 injection has been proposed.
formations.existing_activity: Laboratory carbonation-kinetics studies only.
formations.capacity_basis_research: No basin-scale capacity estimate published; only bench-scale carbonation-efficiency experiments exist (harzburgite ~70% olivine/25% pyroxene/2-3% serpentine; dunite ~97% olivine) showing low carbonation extent for unmilled samples (0.7%) rising sharply with milling (7.4%) in short autoclave tests, illustrating the general kinetic-limitation problem rather than an in-situ reservoir capacity.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Classic, well-preserved Cretaceous ophiolite; harzburgite and dunite exposed extensively in the Troodos massif; degree of serpentinization varies, controlling in-situ reactivity.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Long-studied academically as an ophiolite type-locality; no field-scale CO2 injection proposed to date.
formations.source_research: General Troodos petrology + peridotite carbonation kinetics literature (autoclave carbonation-efficiency studies of Troodos harzburgite/dunite).

formations.name: Turkish Ophiolites (Kizildag / Anatolian belt)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Several Neotethyan ophiolite belts across Anatolia (Kizildag, Pozanti-Karsanti) with variably serpentinized harzburgite and dunite, some showing natural carbonation.
formations.suitability_notes: Geologically comparable to Oman and Albania but unstudied for engineered mineralization.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Turkish ophiolite geology literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 storage capacity study identified.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Multiple Neotethyan ophiolite belts across southern/central Anatolia (Kizildag, Pozanti-Karsanti, others) with harzburgite/dunite bodies, variably serpentinized; some hosting natural travertine/magnesite occurrences indicative of natural carbonation.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Data gap; geologically comparable to other Neotethyan ophiolites (Oman, Albania) but unstudied for engineered mineralization.
formations.source_research: General Turkish ophiolite geology literature; no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Mirdita Ophiolite (Albania) / Balkan Ophiolite Belt
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Large Jurassic harzburgite and dunite massifs in Albania and Greece (Vourinos, Pindos), historically mined for chromite, with natural carbonated serpentinite (listwanite).
formations.suitability_notes: A plausible future European target near Balkan industrial CO2 sources, but no capacity work is published.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Balkan ophiolite geology literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 storage capacity study identified.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Jurassic Mirdita ophiolite (Albania) and related Balkan ophiolite fragments (Vourinos-Greece, Pindos) include large harzburgite/dunite massifs, historically mined for chromite; natural listwanite (carbonated serpentinite) occurrences documented.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Data gap; a plausible future European ISM target given proximity to Balkan industrial CO2 sources, but no capacity work published.
formations.source_research: General Balkan ophiolite geology literature; no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: California Coast Range Ophiolite / Serpentinite belt
formations.capacity_basis: No in-situ capacity study; California serpentinite is discussed mainly for surface carbonation of mine tailings and enhanced weathering.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Coast Range Ophiolite and Franciscan serpentinite bodies (New Idria, Clear Creek) are widely exposed but faulted by the San Andreas system, complicating deep injection.
formations.suitability_notes: Deep injection is little studied because of active faulting and seismicity concerns.
formations.existing_activity: Surface carbonation and enhanced-weathering research on serpentinite mine tailings; no deep in-situ pilot.
formations.source: General California Coast Range Ophiolite geology literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated in-situ CO2 storage capacity study identified; California serpentinite is more often discussed for ex-situ/surficial mineral carbonation (mine tailings, enhanced weathering) than deep in-situ injection.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Coast Range Ophiolite and associated Franciscan Complex serpentinite bodies (including the historic New Idria and Clear Creek serpentinite masses) are extensively exposed but generally structurally complex/faulted (San Andreas system), complicating deep injection.
formations.suitability_notes_research: California's serpentinite is the state rock and a widely cited surficial carbonation research target (Project Vesta-style enhanced weathering, mine tailings carbonation), but in-situ deep injection is less studied than in Oman-analogue settings due to active faulting/seismicity concerns.
formations.existing_activity_research: Surficial/ex-situ carbonation and enhanced-weathering research (e.g. on serpentinite mine tailings); no deep in-situ ISM pilot identified.
formations.source_research: General California Coast Range Ophiolite geology literature; no in-situ mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Bay of Islands Ophiolite (Newfoundland, Canada)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: An Ordovician ophiolite, well exposed in Gros Morne National Park and variably serpentinized.
formations.suitability_notes: A renowned ophiolite type locality, but much of it lies in a protected national park, limiting industrial development.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Bay of Islands ophiolite geology literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 storage capacity study identified.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Classic Ordovician ophiolite complex (harzburgite tectonite plus cumulate sequence), well exposed in Gros Morne National Park; variably serpentinized.
formations.suitability_notes_research: World-renowned type-locality ophiolite used to define oceanic-crust stratigraphy; no engineered CO2 mineralization work identified, and much of it lies within a protected national park, limiting industrial development potential.
formations.source_research: General Bay of Islands ophiolite geology literature; no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: British Columbia Serpentinite Belts (Decar / Cassiar / Shulaps / Atlin)
formations.capacity_basis: No aggregate figure for the belts. A 2024 site-selection study estimates about 0.15-20 Gt CO2 for its three top-ranked sites combined (Shulaps, Coquihalla and Tulameen), depending on method.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: The Decar body contains up to about 13 wt% brucite, which reacts with CO2 even at room temperature. Targets are fractured serpentinite near the surface, not deep supercritical storage.
formations.suitability_notes: CO2 Lock is testing shallow, brucite-targeted carbonation as a lower-cost alternative to deep supercritical injection.
formations.existing_activity: CO2 Lock, an FPX Nickel subsidiary, reported a successful CO2 injection test at its SAM site about 50 km southwest of Prince George in January 2024. A separate UBC and Carbfix study has proposed a pilot in the Coquihalla serpentine belt.
formations.source: CO2 Lock news release 25 Jan 2024 https://www.newsfilecorp.com/release/195720; Steinthorsdottir, Rahimi, Dipple & Snæbjörnsdóttir 2024, Evaluation and site selection for carbon storage via shallow CO2 injection into serpentinite in British Columbia, Canada, Int. J. Greenh. Gas Control, doi:10.1016/j.ijggc.2024.104222; Journal of Petrology 2022 'Formation and Preservation of Brucite and Awaruite...Central British Columbia' https://academic.oup.com/petrology/article/63/11/egac100/6747305
formations.capacity_basis_research: No basin-wide Gt figure published; site-selection studies (2024 ScienceDirect 'Evaluation and site selection for carbon storage via shallow CO2 injection into serpentinite in British Columbia') characterize multiple candidate sites (Decar, Cassiar, Shulaps, Coquihalla, Tulameen, Atlin/Bobtail) rather than producing an aggregate capacity number.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Decar ultramafic body contains up to ~13 wt% brucite (Mg(OH)2) formed during serpentinization - brucite reacts with CO2 even at room temperature, making it a preferred fast-reacting target; fractured serpentinite characterized at multiple sites for near-surface (shallow) CO2 injection rather than deep supercritical storage.
formations.suitability_notes_research: CO2Lock research program (Geoscience BC-funded) is actively piloting shallow, brucite-targeted mineral carbonation as a lower-cost alternative to deep supercritical CO2 injection; listwanite (carbonated serpentinite/quartz-carbonate rock) at Atlin documents natural analogue carbonation. || 2026-10-15 verification: CO2 Lock (FPX Nickel subsidiary) tests shallow brucite-targeted carbonation at SAM; 'Geoscience BC-funded' not verified and removed. Listwanite at Atlin is a natural analogue only.
formations.existing_activity_research: CO2Lock pilot-scale shallow CO2 injection trial at the Atlin/Bobtail site; ongoing site characterization (2019-2025) across multiple BC ultramafic bodies. || 2026-10-15 verification: CO2 Lock SAM site (~50 km SW of Prince George; newsfile 2024-01-25): first CO2 injection into brucite-rich ultramafic rock, field program complete. 'Atlin/Bobtail' removed: neither appears in CO2 Lock/FPX releases. Steinthorsdottir et al. 2024 (IJGGC 104222; EGU24-12878): Shulaps, Coquihalla, Tulameen top-ranked; Coquihalla proposed for pilot. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.source_research: ScienceDirect 2024 'Evaluation and site selection for carbon storage via shallow CO2 injection into serpentinite in British Columbia' https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1750583624001658; Journal of Petrology 2022 'Formation and Preservation of Brucite and Awaruite...Central British Columbia' https://academic.oup.com/petrology/article/63/11/egac100/6747305; ScienceDirect 2025 fractured serpentinite characterization paper https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0883292725002045

formations.name: Thetford Mines / Quebec Asbestos Belt (Appalachian ophiolites)
formations.capacity_basis: No deep-injection capacity study; Quebec asbestos mine tailings have been studied extensively for surface carbonation.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Cambrian-Ordovician serpentinite associated with legacy chrysotile mining, with large volumes of finely milled tailings at the surface.
formations.suitability_notes: Mainly a surface carbonation opportunity using mine tailings rather than a deep injection target.
formations.existing_activity: Tailings carbonation research at Canadian universities; see also the Deep Sky/Carbfix Thetford Mines pilot injection.
formations.source: General Quebec asbestos-belt serpentinite mineral-carbonation literature (tailings carbonation studies).
formations.capacity_basis_research: No in-situ deep injection capacity study identified; Quebec chrysotile (asbestos) mine tailings have instead been studied extensively as an ex-situ/surficial mineral carbonation feedstock (crushed serpentinite tailings react with atmospheric/flue-gas CO2).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Cambrian-Ordovician ophiolitic serpentinite (Thetford Mines, Asbestos/Val-des-Sources) associated with legacy chrysotile mining; large volumes of finely milled tailings already exist at surface.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Primarily an ex-situ mineral carbonation (mine tailings) opportunity rather than a deep in-situ injection target given the milled, surface-stockpiled nature of the resource; included for completeness as part of global ultramafic inventory, capacity distinct in character from deep ISM.
formations.existing_activity_research: Ex-situ tailings carbonation research (various Canadian universities); no deep in-situ ISM pilot.

formations.name: Japan Ophiolites (Hokkaido / Sanbagawa belt)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Several tectonically complex, variably serpentinized ophiolite and serpentinite belts (Hokkaido, Sanbagawa belt, Shikoku).
formations.suitability_notes: Unstudied; Japan's CCS effort focuses on offshore sedimentary basins such as Tomakomai.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Japanese ophiolite geology literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 mineralization capacity study identified.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Multiple accreted ophiolite/serpentinite belts across Japan (Hokkaido, Sanbagawa metamorphic belt, Shikoku); tectonically complex, variably serpentinized.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Data gap; Japan's CCS efforts have focused on offshore sedimentary basins (Tomakomai) rather than onshore ultramafic mineralization.
formations.source_research: General Japanese ophiolite geology literature; no mineralization study identified.

formations.name: Kalimantan / Sulawesi Ophiolites (Indonesia)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Extensive ultramafic complexes in Central Sulawesi and East Kalimantan, heavily weathered at the surface and major nickel ore hosts.
formations.suitability_notes: A large, unassessed resource where regional nickel-mining infrastructure could support mineralization research.
formations.existing_activity: Lab carbonation experiments on regional peridotite (Mount Tawai, Sabah, Malaysia); no in-situ pilot in Indonesia.
formations.source: PMC 2018 'Experimental Investigation and Simplistic Geochemical Modeling of CO2 Mineral Carbonation Using the Mount Tawai Peridotite' https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6273465/
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated CO2 mineralization capacity study identified, despite large lateritized peridotite bodies (also major Ni-laterite ore hosts).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Extensive ultramafic complexes across Central Sulawesi and East Kalimantan (part of the SE Asian ophiolite belt), heavily lateritized at surface; the Mt. Tawai peridotite (Sabah, Malaysia, part of the same regional belt) has been used in lab carbonation-kinetics experiments.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Large, essentially unassessed ultramafic resource; regional Ni-mining infrastructure could potentially be leveraged for co-located mineralization research.
formations.existing_activity_research: Bench-scale carbonation experiments on regional peridotite (e.g. Mt. Tawai, Sabah) but no Indonesia-specific in-situ pilot.

formations.name: Iceland (Carbfix / whole-island basalt)
formations.capacity_basis: Snæbjörnsdóttir and colleagues (2014) estimate about 21-2,470 Gt CO2 for the young basalt of Iceland's active rift zone, depending on method. The 60-7,000 Gt range often quoted for Iceland refers to the offshore ridges (see that panel).
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Young (under 0.8 million years), highly porous basalt in the active rift zone, about a third of Iceland, is the main onshore target; older basalt is less reactive and permeable.
formations.suitability_notes: A demonstrated in-situ mineralization site: Carbfix dissolves CO2 in water before injection, and over 95% mineralizes within about 2 years.
formations.existing_activity: Carbfix has injected at Hellisheiði since 2012, and its Coda Terminal CO2 import hub at Straumsvík is under development.
formations.source: Snæbjörnsdóttir, S.Ó. et al. 2014, CO2 storage potential of basaltic rocks in Iceland and the oceanic ridges, Energy Procedia 63, 4585-4600, doi:10.1016/j.egypro.2014.11.491 (NORDICCS https://www.sintef.no/globalassets/sintef-energi/nordiccs/d-6.1.1407-8-co2-storage-potential-of-basaltic-rocks-in-iceland-and-the-oceanic-ridges_web.pdf); Matter, J.M. et al. 2016 Science (CarbFix mineralization rate)
formations.capacity_basis_research: Snæbjörnsdóttir & Gislason 2016 (and related NORDICCS/SINTEF synthesis) give theoretical storage potential of onshore + offshore Icelandic basalt of roughly 60-7000 Gt CO2, with the upper end reflecting the full basaltic crust volume rather than practically accessible reservoirs. || 2026-10-15 verification: Snæbjörnsdóttir et al. 2014 s5.1: active rift zone ~34,000 km2: 953-2,470 Gt (Reykjanes/Krafla natural analogue, 500-1500 m), ~21 Gt (McGrail method), >400 Gt (Goldberg method); all-Iceland bedrock ~60 Gt (McGrail, Anthonsen et al.) / ~1,200 Gt (Goldberg). s5.2: within 30 km of harbours (~2,390 km2) 67-175 Gt (analogue), 1.4 Gt (McGrail), 28.5 Gt (Goldberg). Previous 60-7,000 Gt was the 2016 OFFSHORE EEZ estimate. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Young (post-glacial, <0.8 Ma), highly porous olivine tholeiite basalt within the active rift zone (~1/3 of Iceland's area) is the most feasible onshore target; older, more altered basalt outside the rift zone is less reactive/permeable.
formations.suitability_notes_research: The world's leading demonstrated ISM site; Carbfix process dissolves CO2 (and H2S) in water before injection, achieving >95% mineralization within ~2 years at the Hellisheiði pilot/commercial site.
formations.existing_activity_research: Carbfix (Hellisheiði geothermal plant, operating since 2012) and Coda Terminal (Straumsvík, import-and-store CO2 hub under development) are the most mature ISM operations globally.

formations.name: East African Rift - Kenya Rift Valley
formations.capacity_basis: No peer-reviewed regional estimate is published; a site study of Olkaria basalt gives 23-89 Mt.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Young rift basalts near Lakes Elementaita and Naivasha share the geothermal systems (Olkaria, Menengai) that supply about half of Kenya's grid, with highly permeable fracture zones.
formations.suitability_notes: Abundant geothermal power for direct air capture is a key economic advantage.
formations.existing_activity: Octavia Carbon and Cella injected about 460 kg of CO2 into basalt near Lake Elementaita in a test reported in May 2026.
formations.source: Carbon Herald 2023 'Cella Sets Sights On Scaling Geologic Carbon Sequestration' https://carbonherald.com/cella-sets-sights-on-scaling-geologic-carbon-sequestration/; Okoko, G.O. & Olaka, L.A. 2021, Can East African rift basalts sequester CO2? Case study of the Kenya rift, Scientific African, doi:10.1016/j.sciaf.2021.e00924; decarbonfuse 5 May 2026 https://decarbonfuse.com/posts/kenya-s-rift-valley-hosts-landmark-dac-to-storage-injection-placing-africa-on-the-carbon-removal-map; MIT Technology Review Dec 2025 (context only) https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/12/22/1130153/geothermal-energy-carbon-capture-kenya-climate-solution/
formations.capacity_basis_research: Widely reported (MIT Technology Review 2025, Cella/decarbonfuse coverage) estimated overall Kenyan Rift Valley storage potential of ~400 Gt CO2; Onyango et al. (ScienceDirect 2021, 'Can East African rift basalts sequester CO2? Case study of the Kenya rift') provides the underlying geological case-study framework. || 2026-10-15 verification: Removed unsupported 50 Gt low and 200 Gt mid. 400 Gt = Cella CEO statement (Carbon Herald 2023-06-05), not MIT TR. Okoko & Olaka 2021 (Sci. Afr., doi:10.1016/j.sciaf.2021.e00924) is a qualitative suitability study. Katana 2025 MSc (Univ. Iceland/GRÓ GTP): Olkaria basalt 23-89 Mt theoretical. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Quaternary-Neogene rift-related basalts and volcaniclastics near Lake Elementaita/Naivasha, associated with the same geothermal reservoirs (Olkaria, Menengai) that supply Kenya's ~50% geothermal grid; high permeability fracture zones in rift-flank basalt.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Paired with abundant local geothermal power (low-carbon energy for DAC) - a key economic advantage; water-alternating-gas (WAG, borrowed from EOR) injection technique demonstrated.
formations.existing_activity_research: Octavia Carbon (DAC) + Cella Mineral Storage: first CO2 mineralization injection in Africa (Project Hummingbird/Jacaranda, near Lake Elementaita), ~460 kg CO2 injected in initial test (2024-2025); 'Great Carbon Valley' scale-up plans reported by MIT Technology Review (Dec 2025). || 2026-10-15 verification: Octavia Carbon (DAC) + Cella: ~460 kg pure-phase CO2 injected into basalt near Lake Elementaita using water-alternating-gas (decarbonfuse, 2026-05-05). Earlier '2024-2025' date was wrong.

formations.name: East African Rift - Ethiopia / Djibouti (Afar Depression)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Very high geothermal gradients and active volcanism (Erta Ale, Dabbahu) give reactive, permeable young basalt but hard drilling conditions: extreme heat, remoteness and volcanic hazard.
formations.suitability_notes: Geologically analogous to the Kenya rift and Iceland but essentially unstudied for CO2 storage.
formations.existing_activity: None known for CO2 mineralization; geothermal exploration is ongoing in Djibouti and Ethiopia.
formations.source: General Afar Depression volcanology/rift literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated capacity study identified; the Afar Depression sits atop both the Oligocene Ethiopian/Yemen flood-basalt pile and actively rifting, highly fractured young basalt at the Africa-Arabia-Somali triple junction.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Very high geothermal gradient and active volcanism (Erta Ale, Dabbahu) provide highly reactive, permeable young basalt, but also challenging drilling conditions (extreme heat, remoteness, seismic/volcanic hazard).
formations.suitability_notes_research: Geologically analogous to the Kenya rift and Iceland (active rift basalt) but essentially unstudied for CCS; flagged as a plausible future extension of the Kenya rift ISM model.
formations.existing_activity_research: None known for CO2 mineralization; geothermal exploration ongoing (Djibouti, Ethiopia).
formations.source_research: General Afar Depression volcanology/rift literature; no CO2 mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Hawaii (Island of Hawaii basalt shield volcanoes)
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Very young, highly permeable shield-volcano basalt (Mauna Loa, Kilauea) with vesicular flow tops and lava tubes; active volcanic and seismic hazard constrains siting.
formations.suitability_notes: A promising geological analogue to Iceland, but volcanic hazard and a lack of large local CO2 sources limit near-term relevance.
formations.existing_activity: None known.
formations.source: General Hawaiian volcanology
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated in-situ mineralization capacity study identified; discussion of Hawaiian basalt in the CCS literature is largely conceptual (young, highly porous ocean-island tholeiite/alkalic basalt analogous to Iceland).
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Extremely young, highly permeable shield-volcano basalt (Mauna Loa, Kilauea) with abundant vesicular flow tops and lava tubes; active volcanic/seismic hazard is a major siting constraint.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Geologically promising analogue to Iceland's young rift basalt, but active-volcano hazard and lack of large local point-source CO2 emitters limit near-term relevance; a research/data gap.
formations.source_research: General Hawaiian volcanology; no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Japan / Kurile Volcanic Arc Basalts
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity study; arc basalts and andesites are less magnesium-rich, and so less reactive per unit volume, than rift basalts or peridotite.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Calc-alkaline to tholeiitic arc volcanics with variable porosity.
formations.suitability_notes: A lower-priority target because its chemistry is less favorable than that of flood or rift basalts and peridotite.
formations.existing_activity: None known for mineralization.
formations.source: General arc volcanism/geochemistry literature
formations.capacity_basis_research: No dedicated capacity study identified; arc basalts/andesites are generally less Mg-rich and thus less reactive per unit volume than rift tholeiites or peridotite.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Calc-alkaline to tholeiitic arc volcanics, variable porosity; Japan's main CCS focus (Tomakomai) targets offshore sedimentary aquifers, not arc basalt mineralization.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Lower priority ISM target given less favorable (more silicic, less Mg/Ca-rich) bulk chemistry than true flood/rift basalts or peridotite; included for completeness/data-gap tracking.
formations.source_research: General arc volcanism/geochemistry literature; no mineralization capacity study identified.

formations.name: Juan de Fuca Plate (offshore Pacific Northwest)
formations.capacity_basis: Goldberg and Slagle (2008) give at least about 245 Gt CO2 for the 245,000 km2 ridge region, up to about 2,450 Gt for thicker, more porous reservoir. Goldberg and colleagues (2008) give about 760-920 Gt CO2 for a 78,000 km2 area meeting depth and sediment-cover criteria.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Sub-seafloor pillow basalts with porosity up to about 20%, sealed by thick, low-permeability sediment, with several reinforcing trapping mechanisms.
formations.suitability_notes: A well-studied offshore basalt target, though deepwater drilling and monitoring make costs far higher than for onshore saline storage.
formations.existing_activity: The Cascadia CarbonSAFE pre-feasibility study evaluated a 50 Mt, 20-year injection program on the eastern ridge flank; no injection yet.
formations.source: Goldberg, D.S., Takahashi, T. & Slagle, A.L. 2008, Carbon dioxide sequestration in deep-sea basalt, PNAS 105, 9920-9925, doi:10.1073/pnas.0804397105; Goldberg, D. & Slagle, A. 2008, A global assessment of deep-sea basalt sites for carbon sequestration, Nature Precedings, doi:10.1038/npre.2008.2640.1 (published in Energy Procedia 1, 3675-3682, 2009); Fairley, J., McLing, T. & Podgorney, R. 2013, Sub-seafloor carbon dioxide storage potential on the Juan de Fuca plate, western North America, Energy Procedia 37, 5248-5257 (simulation study); Columbia Climate School Cascadia Basin pre-feasibility project https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/view/1019
formations.capacity_basis_research: Goldberg et al. (2008, 2010) estimate total volume potential of the eastern + western Juan de Fuca Ridge flanks at 134-668 Gt-C (gigatonnes of carbon, for 20-100 m net reservoir thickness); converting Gt-C to GtCO2 (x3.67) gives roughly 490-2450 Gt CO2. A more conservative, commonly cited figure is 'at least 229 billion tonnes of carbon' (~840 Gt CO2) for the plate as a whole. || 2026-10-15 verification: Goldberg, Takahashi & Slagle 2008 PNAS: 78,000 km2 filtered area, 780 km3 pore volume, 208 Gt C (liquid) to ~250 Gt C (carbonate); 229 Gt C = midpoint (~840 Gt CO2), used as mid. Goldberg & Slagle 2008 (Nature Precedings poster; Energy Procedia 2009): Juan de Fuca Ridge region 244,963 km2, pore volume 245-2,450 km3 (20-100 m, 5-10%); 67 Gt C minimum; ~134-670 Gt C at 10% porosity is MY conversion (490-2,450 km3 x 0.273 g C/cm3), not a stated source figure. Conversions x3.664. Previous low 490 used the 10% case only; 'more conservative plate-wide 229 Gt C' wording was wrong. 'Goldberg 2010' citation was Fairley et al. 2013 (no capacity). Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Sub-seafloor pillow basalts with interconnected high-permeability zones and porosity up to ~20%; overlain by thick, low-permeability sediment providing a natural seal; multiple trapping mechanisms (hydrodynamic, CO2-density inversion at depth, and mineralization) reinforce containment.
formations.suitability_notes_research: One of the best-characterized offshore basalt targets globally; the Cascadia CarbonSAFE pre-feasibility study evaluated a 50 Mt CO2 / 20-year injection program on the eastern ridge flank ~200 miles offshore Washington/BC. Major caveat: offshore basalt storage is expected to cost far more than onshore saline-aquifer storage, due to deepwater drilling and monitoring costs.
formations.existing_activity_research: Cascadia CarbonSAFE pre-feasibility study (Columbia Climate School / industry partners); no injection yet.
formations.source_research: Goldberg, D.S. et al. 2008 PNAS 'Carbon dioxide sequestration in deep-sea basalt'; Goldberg, D.S. et al. 2010 'Sub-seafloor Carbon Dioxide Storage Potential on the Juan de Fuca Plate' https://www.researchgate.net/publication/270955080_Sub-seafloor_Carbon_Dioxide_Storage_Potential_on_the_Juan_de_Fuca_Plate_Western_North_America; Columbia Climate School Cascadia Basin pre-feasibility project https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/view/1019

formations.name: Cascadia Basin / Offshore Washington-British Columbia sedimented basalt
formations.capacity_basis: A subset of the Juan de Fuca Plate estimate (see that panel); the CarbonSAFE target was a 50 Mt, 20-year injection program, far below the regional theoretical ceiling.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Basalt basement under about 2600 m of water, with interflow reservoirs beneath several hundred meters of sealing sediment.
formations.suitability_notes: A project-scale target that shows the gap between Gt-scale theoretical and Mt-scale project numbers.
formations.existing_activity: Cascadia CarbonSAFE integrated pre-feasibility study completed; no injection to date.
formations.source: Columbia Climate School project page https://people.climate.columbia.edu/projects/view/1019
formations.capacity_basis_research: Subset of the broader Juan de Fuca plate assessment (see above); the specific CarbonSAFE pre-feasibility target was a 50 Mt CO2 (0.05 Gt) 20-year injection program, far below the regional theoretical ceiling.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Sediment-covered basalt basement, ~2600 m water depth, targeted interflow basalt reservoirs beneath several hundred meters of sediment (which also serves as a seal).
formations.suitability_notes_research: Practically-scoped, near-term project distinct from the plate-wide theoretical estimate; illustrates the gap between theoretical (Gt-scale) and project-scale (Mt-scale) numbers.

formations.name: Reykjanes Ridge / Offshore Iceland Mid-Atlantic Ridge basalt
formations.capacity_basis: Snæbjörnsdóttir and Gislason (2016) estimate 60-7,000 Gt CO2 for a 93,000 km2 strip along the Reykjanes and Kolbeinsey ridges within Iceland's exclusive economic zone, depending on method. These are theoretical figures with no site-specific data.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Young, porous basalt on an actively spreading ridge directly offshore southwest Iceland, in shallower water than typical ridges because of the Iceland hotspot.
formations.suitability_notes: Young basalt along a slow-spreading ridge in relatively shallow water close to Iceland. A German-led research project (AIMS3) is assessing it for future CO2 injection.
formations.existing_activity: Research boreholes and monitoring equipment have been installed on the ridge flank; no CO2 has been injected.
formations.source: Snæbjörnsdóttir, S.Ó. & Gislason, S.R. 2016, CO2 storage potential of basaltic rocks offshore Iceland, Energy Procedia 86, 371-380, doi:10.1016/j.egypro.2016.01.038; Kopf, A. et al. 2024, Initial results of a pilot project for sub-seabed basalt storage of carbon dioxide on the Reykjanes Ridge, Carbon Capture Sci. Technol. 13, 100265, doi:10.1016/j.ccst.2024.100265
formations.capacity_basis_research: Included within the broader Snæbjörnsdóttir & Gislason (2016) 60-7000 Gt Iceland+ridges estimate; a dedicated sub-seabed pilot on the Reykjanes Ridge itself has begun (2024 ScienceDirect paper on initial pilot results). || 2026-10-15 verification: Snæbjörnsdóttir & Gislason 2016 Energy Procedia 86:371-380 (doi:10.1016/j.egypro.2016.01.038): offshore Iceland EEZ strip 30 km each side of Reykjanes + Kolbeinsey ridge axes, <3 Ma, ~93,000 km2. Scenarios: 60 (McGrail), 1,100 (Goldberg), 2,600 / 6,800 (Reykjanes / Krafla natural analogue). This range was previously, wrongly, also applied to onshore Iceland. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Actively spreading mid-ocean ridge basalt, young and porous, directly offshore SW Iceland; shallower water depth than typical mid-ocean-ridge settings due to the Iceland hotspot's ridge elevation.
formations.suitability_notes_research: First sub-seabed basalt CO2 storage pilot on an active mid-ocean ridge segment; extends the onshore Carbfix approach offshore.
formations.existing_activity_research: Pilot project for sub-seabed basalt storage of CO2 on the Reykjanes Ridge (initial results reported 2024).
formations.source_research: ScienceDirect 2024 'Initial results of a pilot project for sub-seabed basalt storage of carbon dioxide on the Reykjanes Ridge' https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772656824000770

formations.name: Mid-Atlantic Ridge and global mid-ocean ridge system (generic offshore basalt)
formations.capacity_basis: Snæbjörnsdóttir and colleagues (2014) estimate about 2,000 to 100,000 Gt CO2 for the global ridge system, depending on method. These are whole-system theoretical figures, not site or economic estimates.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Ridge basalt is young, porous and reactive near spreading centers but largely inaccessible, under 2000-4000+ m of water and far from shore and CO2 sources.
formations.suitability_notes: Essentially no near-term practical relevance given extreme cost and distance.
formations.existing_activity: None; a research project has drilled monitoring boreholes on the Reykjanes Ridge flank, but no CO2 has been injected (see that panel).
formations.source: Snæbjörnsdóttir, S.Ó. et al. 2014, CO2 storage potential of basaltic rocks in Iceland and the oceanic ridges, Energy Procedia 63, 4585-4600, doi:10.1016/j.egypro.2014.11.491 (NORDICCS version https://www.sintef.no/globalassets/sintef-energi/nordiccs/d-6.1.1407-8-co2-storage-potential-of-basaltic-rocks-in-iceland-and-the-oceanic-ridges_web.pdf); Goldberg, D. & Slagle, A. 2008, A global assessment of deep-sea basalt sites for carbon sequestration, Nature Precedings, doi:10.1038/npre.2008.2640.1
formations.capacity_basis_research: SINTEF/NORDICCS synthesis (Snæbjörnsdóttir & Gislason 2016 and related work) states mid-ocean ridges worldwide could store 'up to 100,000 Gt CO2' in principle - an extreme upper-bound, whole-ridge-system theoretical figure, not a site-specific or economically meaningful estimate. || 2026-10-15 verification: Snæbjörnsdóttir et al. 2014 (Energy Procedia 63:4585; NORDICCS D6.1.1407(8)) s5.3: ~2,000 Gt (McGrail assumptions), ~40,000 Gt (Goldberg assumptions), 100,000-250,000 Gt (Icelandic analogue). Previous 1,000 low / 30,000 mid had no source; 100,000 was mislabelled as an upper bound and misattributed to Snæbjörnsdóttir & Gislason 2016. Goldberg & Slagle 2008: 4,119 Gt C minimum for 15 deep-sea sites (x3.664 = ~15,100 Gt CO2). Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Global mid-ocean ridge system basalt is universally young, porous, and reactive near spreading centers, but almost entirely inaccessible at present due to water depth (typically 2000-4000+ m) and distance from shore/CO2 sources.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Included as the theoretical global offshore-basalt ceiling referenced in the literature; essentially zero near-term practical relevance given extreme cost/distance.
formations.existing_activity_research: None (conceptual estimate only, apart from the localized Reykjanes Ridge pilot listed separately).

formations.name: Kerguelen Plateau (Southern Indian Ocean)
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity study; a very large igneous province, but remote, in deep water and far from CO2 sources.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Cretaceous submarine plateau basalt, mostly under 1000-2000 m of water and unexplored as a reservoir.
formations.suitability_notes: Shows the gap between global mafic rock volume and any realistically deployable subset; no practical near-term relevance.
formations.existing_activity: None.
formations.source: General Kerguelen Plateau geology literature (Frey et al., Coffin & Eldholm LIP reviews)
formations.capacity_basis_research: No CO2 storage capacity study identified; the Kerguelen Plateau is one of the largest Large Igneous Provinces on Earth by volume (oceanic plateau basalt), but it is remote, deep-water, and has no nearby CO2 point sources.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Submarine oceanic plateau basalt (Cretaceous), water depths mostly 1000-2000 m over the plateau itself; essentially unexplored for reservoir engineering purposes.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Included as a data-gap entry illustrating the scale mismatch between total global mafic rock volume and any realistically deployable subset; no practical near-term relevance.
formations.source_research: General Kerguelen Plateau geology literature (Frey et al., Coffin & Eldholm LIP reviews); no CO2 storage study identified.

formations.name: Harrat Al-Shaam / Arabian Harrat Basalt Fields (Saudi Arabia, Jordan)
formations.capacity_basis: No capacity estimate has been published for the harrat basalt fields. The nearest figure, about 4.2 Gt CO2 for older Oligocene basalts near Jizan in southwest Saudi Arabia (Oelkers and colleagues 2022), covers a different formation.
formations.depth_porosity_notes: Cenozoic basalt fields (harrats) with vesicular, permeable flow tops between denser flow interiors.
formations.suitability_notes: Part of Saudi Arabia's CCS ambitions, with KAUST adapting Iceland's Carbfix approach to Arabian basalt.
formations.existing_activity: Laboratory studies by KAUST and others. The KAUST and Aramco field pilot at Jizan was in separate, older basalts (see the Jizan project).
formations.source: ScienceDirect 2022 'The subsurface carbonation potential of basaltic rocks from the Jizan region' https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1750583622001906; KAUST 'Storing Saudi Arabia's CO2' https://fii.kaust.edu.sa/en/energy-industrial-leadership/storing-saudi-arabia-c02/; ScienceDirect 2025 Harrat Al-Shaam Jordan study https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2666261225000239; SPE 2025 Harrat Rahat scoriaceous basalt paper
formations.capacity_basis_research: Jizan region (SW Saudi Arabia) Oligocene basaltic rocks estimated at ~4.2 Gt CO2 total mineralization capacity, framed as sufficient for >100 years of regional industrial emissions; broader Harrat Al-Shaam basalt field (spanning Jordan/Saudi Arabia/Syria) and Harrat Rahat/Harrat Uwayrid are separately being assessed (2023-2025 studies) but not yet combined into one figure - low/high bounds here are an illustrative range pending a basin-wide synthesis. || 2026-10-15 verification: Removed illustrative 1-10 Gt range (no source). Oelkers et al. 2022 IJGGC 120:103772 ~4.2 Gt CO2 applies to Jizan Oligocene rift basalts (~16.9N 42.6E), not the Cenozoic harrats (Al-Shaam, Rahat, Uwayrid), which have only lab studies. Option: add Jizan as its own formation (capacity 4.2 Gt) if the user wants it mapped. Verified 2026-10-15.
formations.depth_porosity_notes_research: Cenozoic alkali/scoriaceous basalt fields (harrats) with vesicular, permeable flow tops interbedded with denser flow interiors; KAUST-led wettability/nanofluid-treatment studies characterize CO2/brine/basalt interfacial properties relevant to trapping capacity.
formations.suitability_notes_research: Part of the Saudi Green Initiative's CCS ambitions; KAUST explicitly frames its program as adapting the Icelandic Carbfix approach to Arabian basalt.
formations.existing_activity_research: Laboratory characterization (KAUST, various 2022-2025 papers on Jizan, Harrat Uwayrid, Harrat Rahat basalts); no field pilot yet identified. || 2026-10-15 verification: KAUST laboratory characterization (Harrat Uwayrid, Harrat Rahat, Jizan basalts, 2022-2025); the KAUST/Aramco Jizan field pilot (about 131 t CO2, 2024-25, Nature 2026) is in the separate Jizan Oligocene basalts, not the harrats.
